The Case for Complete Deregulation: Pornography and the Right to Absolute Free Expression

    The notion that adult sexual imagery should be subject to unique legal fetters is a relic of paternalistic morality and a direct assault on the core promise of an open society: that each adult is sovereign over mind, body, and consensual exchange. Not partial reform, not “within reasonable limits,” but an unconditional repeal of all obscenity statutes, age-verification mandates, criminal producers’ liabilities, zoning laws, and government-content-rating boards. The argument rests on three pillars: (1) individual autonomy as the supreme ethical imperative; (2) the First Amendment’s absolute protection of expression; and (3) practical reality: prohibition has never suppressed demand— it only suppresses safety, diversity, and dignity.

  2. Moral Individualism and Bodily Sovereignty
    At the moral center is a simple truth: consenting adults own their bodies and imaginations. This ownership confers a plenary right to depict, view, and trade whatever fantasies they choose, provided the acts themselves involve willing participants and competent decision-making. All collectivist objections—whether couched in “community standards,” “public morals,” or “human dignity”—reduce human beings to wards of the state. If a legislature may forbid the representation of penetration, it may tomorrow forbid the representation of protest, prayer, or scientific dissent on the pretext that each too “debases” some alleged civic virtue. Remove the community veto and affirm the personal veto: a citizen may click away or close the tab.

  3. Free Speech Absolutism
    The First Amendment does not orbit around political discourse’s solar center. It is a total repudiation of prerogative censorship. Justice Hugo Black’s maxim—​“no law means no law”​—tolerates no asterisk for erotic words or images. Speech is either protected absolutely or it is protected politically. When courts carve out an obscenity exception, they empower prosecutors and judges to become national film editors, deciding which combinations of filmed flesh cross an ineffable line. Every such ruling invites viewpoint discrimination: depictions of missionary marital sex remain “tolerable,” depictions of queer kink invite raids. The First Amendment is binary: on or off. Total abolition of obscenity laws restores that switch to its rightful “on” position for every genre, lighting level, and camera angle.

    Prohibitionists claim to “protect women,” yet raids historically entrench patriarchy. Early-twentieth-century police shut down birth-control pamphlets as “obscene,” driving Margaret Sanger’s maternal-health advocacy underground. Presently, regulations disproportionately target queer and BIPOC producers whose aesthetics unsettle white-supremacist norms. A Black trans dominatrix broadcasting consensual power exchange finds her bank account closed under “morals clauses,” while multinational cable networks air heteronormative ads framed identically. Repeal liberates the expressive margins from the double bind of respectability politics, allowing authentic sexual narratives by and for historically silenced bodies.

  5. Harm Reduction, Not Moral Panic
    Child-sexual-abuse material is already violence itself, not speech, and its criminalization is unchallenged here; coercion of adults is likewise assault. But adult obscenity laws conflate all erotica with non-consensual crimes. The empirical record shows the inverse: open, legal adult industries reliably self-regulate. Performers’ unions negotiate condom use, mental-health contracts, and residual payments—whereas criminalized street trade offers zero health infrastructure. After Denmark’s 1969 abolition of obscenity laws, sex-crime rates fell. After U.S. jurisdictions implement criminal-record checks for producers (instead of prohibition), labor violations plummet. Sunshine, not darkness, codifies consent.

  6. Dynamic Economic Liberty
    Pornography is not merely culture; it is commerce. Every attempt to channel erotic labor into untraceable black markets dynamites tax bases, undermines labor rights, and gifts earnings to cartels. A fully deregulated adult sector would pay income taxes, carry liability insurance, be scrutinized under ordinary labor or antitrust rules like any industry. Performers could unionize, sue wage thieves, and secure residuals via intellectual-property law. Politicians who thunder against adult platforms happily subsidize coal and gambling interests—asserting economic ethics that only apply when the product offends their blushes, not their budgets.

  7. Digital Realities Make Prohibition Impossible
    The internet already enforces what legislators cannot: near-frictionless global access. Every firewall, credit-card blockade, or state-law age gate is bypassed by millions of teenagers with a VPN. Obsession with “think of the children” masks the true objective—moral policing of adults. Banning a Tumblr blog merely metastasizes it onto offshore servers beyond U.S. labor standards, safety protocols, and tax jurisdiction. Under deregulation, platforms headquartered in the United States would innovate transparency tools rather than perma-panic about the next compliance deadline. SESTA/FOSTA—legislation touted to “end trafficking”—has in fact endangered consensual sex workers by shuttering advertising venues that once allowed client screening. Liberty would reverse this humanitarian catastrophe.

  8. Precedent, Parity, and the Slippery Slope in Reverse
    If the state can yank a vibrator off a streaming service today, tomorrow it can police comic books, romance novels, or reproductive-health diagrams. The Intellectual Freedom Clause is not a menu; it is a firewall. Repeal one brick and the structure tumbles. Conversely, absolute abolition of obscenity laws raises the constitutional bar against future speech restrictions. The slope runs away from tyranny rather than toward it.

  9. Answering the Standard Counter-Arguments

  • “Porn demeans women”: Choose the women. Performers routinely testify that regulation, not expression, demeans—via lost banking, eviction, or police profiling.
  • “Creates unrealistic expectations”: So do cologne ads. Adulthood implies media literacy.
  • “Addiction”: We do not ban alcohol, video games, or social media because some misuse them. Harm-reduction education suffices.
  • “Sex trafficking”: Criminalization colludes with traffickers by isolating victims from formal complaint channels; legal industries foster whistle-blowing protocols.

  1. A Call for Legislative and Judicial Action

Courts should grant certiorari to any remaining states’ cases and declare obscenity criteria facially unconstitutional. Municipalities must end discriminatory zoning that exiles adult stores while welcoming liquor shops next door. American civil society then inherits a genuine marketplace of ideas—including the bedroom ones.

  2. Conclusion
    Freedom requires courage to relinquish the policing of imagination. Pornography offends some; that is the ante in pluralism. Power to regulate comes dressed as caretaker but always acts as censor. By eradicating every obscenity law, the republic finally consummates its founding promise: no sovereign between mind and image, no warden between body and screen.

In a society that claims to cherish liberty, the regulation of pornography through obscenity laws and content restrictions represents an indefensible overreach. Forcing adults to submit their intimate imaginations to obscenity tests revives the same logic once used to ban Ulysses or Lady Chatterley's Lover, works now recognized as literature.

Speech about sex receives no lesser protection than speech about politics or science. The market, technology, reputation, and personal discernment regulate far more responsively than distant officials.

This position is not permissive indulgence but logical entailment of free society. Pornography regulation is not peripheral; it reveals whether a polity privileges individual conscience or collective moral supervision. John Stuart Mill's harm principle provides the essential framework for understanding why obscenity laws cannot be justified in a free society. Mill argued that the only legitimate reason for restricting individual liberty is to prevent direct harm to others. Crucially, offense, disgust, or moral disapproval do not constitute harm in this framework. When applied to pornography, this principle reveals that consensually produced adult content, regardless of how offensive some may find it, causes no direct harm to non-participants and therefore falls outside the legitimate scope of government regulation.

The consumption of pornography is fundamentally a private act that affects only willing participants. The Constitutional Argument: First Amendment Absolutism

The First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution states unequivocally that "Congress shall make no law... abridging the freedom of speech." This language contains no exceptions for sexual content, and the Supreme Court's creation of an "obscenity exception" represents judicial overreach that undermines the amendment's clear meaning. As Justice Hugo Black argued in his dissents, the First Amendment's language is absolute, and courts have no authority to create categories of unprotected speech based on content.

The current Miller test for obscenity, which considers whether material appeals to "prurient interest" and lacks "serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value," is inherently subjective and grants government officials dangerous discretion to act as arbiters of taste. This subjectivity has led to the censorship of works by James Joyce, D.H. Lawrence, and countless other artists whose contributions to culture are now widely recognized. The history of obscenity prosecution demonstrates that such laws inevitably target unpopular minorities and emerging art forms rather than protecting any legitimate public interest.

The Practical Argument: The Failure and Costs of Regulation

Beyond principled objections, the practical case against obscenity laws is overwhelming. In the digital age, attempts to regulate pornography have proven both futile and counterproductive. The internet has made pornographic content ubiquitous and easily accessible regardless of local laws, rendering enforcement efforts expensive exercises in futility.

Moreover, criminalization drives the industry underground, making it harder to ensure performer safety and consent. Critics of deregulation often raise concerns about pornography's alleged social harms, including claims about addiction, relationship effects, and objectification. However, these arguments fail for several reasons:

The Case for Complete Deregulation of Pornography: A Defense of Absolute Expression

Introduction

For decades, governments across the world have imposed restrictions on sexually explicit material under the guise of protecting public morality, shielding minors, and preserving "community standards." Yet these obscenity laws, regardless of the intentions behind them, represent one of the most insidious forms of censorship in modern democratic societies. The time has come for their complete abolition. Not reform. Not modification. Abolition. Every legal restriction on pornographic content—whether framed as obscenity, indecency, or moral endangerment—violates the foundational principles of free expression, adult autonomy, and human dignity that democratic societies are supposed to uphold.

This essay argues, without equivocation, that all government restrictions on pornographic content should be dismantled. The arguments that follow are not hedged with caveats or softened by compromise. They represent a principled, consistent application of what genuine freedom of expression requires.

I. The Logical Foundation: Free Speech Must Be Absolute or It Is Nothing

The most powerful argument for deregulation rests on a simple but devastating logical point: free speech, if it is to mean anything, cannot have a content-based exception for sexuality. When we permit the government to prohibit speech merely because a majority finds it offensive, disgusting, or morally objectionable, we have abandoned the principle of free expression entirely.

The American legal scholar and justice Oliver Wendell Holmes famously warned that the protection of free speech "would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic." This exception is often cited to justify content-based restrictions, but it proves too much. The "shouting fire" example concerns direct, immediate, physical harm to identifiable persons—it is a narrow exception about fraud and incitement, not about offense, discomfort, or moral disapproval.

Obscenity laws, by contrast, prohibit speech that causes no such harm. The material depicts or describes acts that, between consenting adults, are perfectly legal. A film showing two adults engaged in consensual sex is not analogous to a fraudulent cry of "fire" in a crowded theater. It harms no one. The only "harm" is to sensibilities—and protecting sensibilities is the work of prudes, not the business of a free society.

The philosopher John Stuart Mill articulated this principle more than 160 years ago in On Liberty: "The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others." Mill's harm principle is not a libertarian addendum to free speech theory; it is its core. If we accept that government may suppress speech solely because it depicts acts that are themselves legal, we have created a category of forbidden thought and representation—a category that has no principled limit. Once we accept that the state may ban words and images about legal conduct because some citizens find those words and images offensive, we have given the state permission to ban anything, provided enough people are sufficiently offended.

II. The Practical Failures of Obscenity Law

Even if one were to ignore the principled arguments, the practical track record of obscenity enforcement demonstrates that such laws are not merely philosophically wrong but functionally catastrophic.

Selective and Capricious Enforcement. Obscenity laws are enforced almost entirely against the disfavored. Wealthy, mainstream publishers can often escape prosecution; small distributors and producers are crushed. The "community standards" test—which asks whether the average person, applying contemporary standards, would find the work appeals to "prurient interest"—is the antithesis of the rule of law. It hands prosecutors arbitrary power to enforce their personal aesthetic and moral judgments. The same photograph may be perfectly legal in Amsterdam and a felony in Alabama, and the same work may be prosecuted today and protected tomorrow based on nothing more than shifting cultural winds.

Inability to Reduce Demand. Decades of evidence demonstrate that obscenity laws do not reduce the production, distribution, or consumption of pornography. They merely push it into more dangerous and exploitative channels. The most restrictive regimes—where pornography is illegal—are not the societies with the least consumption; they are societies where the industry operates without accountability, where workers have no legal protections, and where dangerous content proliferates because no oversight exists. Where porn is legal and regulated as a business, labor standards, health testing, and consent verification become possible. Where it is illegal, none of these things exist.

The Internet Has Rendered Geographic Regulation Impossible. Most importantly, in the twenty-first century, the obscenity framework is not just morally wrong but practically absurd. A film produced legally in one country is available in every country on earth within seconds. National governments cannot enforce content restrictions against global digital content without transforming themselves into surveillance states. The choice is binary: either accept that the material exists and will be accessed, or build the infrastructure of totalitarianism. No serious person can want the latter. The former requires deregulation.

III. The Censorship of Knowledge and Health

Obscenity laws do not merely restrict entertainment. They suppress information critical to human health, dignity, and safety.

Comprehensive, accurate sexual education is one of the most powerful public health interventions available. It reduces rates of teen pregnancy, sexually transmitted infection, and sexual violence. Yet under the same legal framework that prohibits "obscene" content, the production of explicit educational material becomes a legally perilous endeavor. Researchers, sex educators, and public health professionals have documented that over-broad obscenity laws have a chilling effect on legitimate sexual health communication, on materials aimed at helping survivors of sexual violence process their experiences, on LGBTQ+ resources, and on the documentation of sexual subcultures for academic study.

What is "obscene" in this context? The line between education and obscenity is drawn by prosecutors and judges applying subjective standards. When a medical textbook includes detailed anatomical illustrations, it is safe. When a sex education website uses the same illustrations in a different context, it may be prosecutable. This is not a system designed to protect anyone; it is a system designed to enforce conformity to a particular vision of sexuality that the state has deemed appropriate.

IV. The Historical Record: Censorship as Oppression

Anyone who has studied the history of obscenity law in practice should be deeply suspicious of it. Obscenity laws have been used to:

  • Prosecute works of profound literary and artistic merit, including Ulysses by James Joyce, Lady Chatterley's Lover by D.H. Lawrence, Lolita by Vladimir Nabokov, and the photography of Robert Mapplethorpe.
  • Suppress LGBTQ+ content for most of the twentieth century, treating depictions of same-sex love as obscene even as heterosexual equivalents were tolerated. The harm here was not to "community standards" but to a community of people denied the ability to see themselves represented.
  • Criminalize sex-positive feminist literature during the so-called "sex wars," in which feminist and queer authors were prosecuted under obscenity statutes for their attempts to reclaim sexual imagery.
  • Target marginalized creators while mainstream commercial pornography often escaped scrutiny. The Department of Justice under multiple administrations has pursued small, queer, and feminist producers while allowing industry giants to operate.

This is not an accident. Obscenity law is a tool of social control, and it is wielded most aggressively against those whose sexuality and expression challenge the prevailing moral order.

V. Age Verification, Consent, and the False Equivalence

Those who oppose deregulation often retreat to one argument: "But what about the children? What about exploitation?" These concerns are real, and they are not arguments against the deregulation of pornography. They are arguments for the regulation of who creates it, under what conditions, and who may access it.

It is perfectly possible—and desirable—to have laws that:

  • Prohibit the production of pornography involving minors, with severe penalties.
  • Require verification of age for performers in legal adult content.
  • Combat human trafficking and coercion through labor protections and criminal penalties directed at perpetrators.
  • Mandate health and safety standards in the industry.

None of these require content-based prohibitions on what consenting adults may create, view, or distribute. Indeed, the existence of a legal, regulated industry is the only reliable way to enforce these protections. Underground industries have no compliance mechanisms, no labor inspectors, and no accountability. A society that cares about exploitation should want pornography above ground, not below it.

The argument that deregulating pornography will "lead to" child sexual abuse material is a sleight of hand. Child sexual abuse material is already illegal everywhere, and it is not "pornography" in any morally defensible sense—it is documentary evidence of a crime. We do not "regulate" murder by restricting the depiction of violence in fiction. We do not "deregulate" theft by removing restrictions on depictions of theft in films. The existence of criminal acts in the world does not justify the prohibition of fiction or consensual representation.

VI. Bodily Autonomy and Adult Sovereignty

At its deepest level, the case for deregulation rests on the principle of adult sovereignty over one's own body and mind. Adults have the right to make decisions about their own sexuality, their own relationships, and their own exposure to sexual material. This includes the right to consume material that others find offensive, shocking, or degrading to their sense of human dignity.

A society that permits the state to dictate what sexual images its citizens may view is a society that has abandoned the concept of the adult citizen. It treats people as children requiring state protection from their own choices, or as moral agents who can be trusted with the vote, the family, the workplace, and the military, but cannot be trusted with the contents of their own minds.

This is profoundly dehumanizing. The deepest principle of liberal democracy is that adults are sovereign over their own lives. The state may legitimately restrict action that harms others; it may not restrict thought, imagination, or private consumption.

VII. The Slippery Slope Is Real—But It Runs the Other Way

Critics of deregulation often invoke the "slippery slope" argument: if we permit all pornography, what next? But the empirical slope runs in the opposite direction. Once a society accepts the principle that the state may ban depictions of legal conduct because they are "obscene," there is no logical stopping point. The same principle has been used to ban depictions of drug use, of suicide, of blasphemy, of political dissent, of homosexuality, of "subversive" art, of contraception, of interracial relationships, of unmarried women expressing desire, and on, and on.

The principle is the danger, not the specific content it is currently used to target. Every time we accept an obscenity prosecution, we strengthen a framework that has historically been used to crush the marginalized, the dissident, and the merely different. The slope is real—and it leads straight to comprehensive thought control.

Conclusion: A Demand for Moral Courage

The complete deregulation of pornography is not a radical position. It is the only position consistent with the principles that democratic societies claim to hold. Every argument offered in defense of obscenity laws—that they protect morality, shield children, preserve community standards—either fails on its own terms or can be addressed by means that do not require content-based suppression.

We do not need the state to protect us from the contents of our own minds. We do not need prosecutors to tell us which consensual adult acts we may see depicted. We do not need "community standards" enforced by men with badges. We need a legal framework that protects the vulnerable, prosecutes actual crimes, and leaves adults free to live, think, and create as they choose—including, yes, sexually.

A society that fears the sexual imagination of its citizens is a society that has lost faith in its own principles. The abolition of obscenity laws is not a concession to prurience; it is a defense of the most fundamental freedom there is: the freedom to think, to see, and to imagine, free from the coercive hand of the state.

Arguments for Abolishing Obscenity Laws: A Free-Expression Perspective

This is a position advocated by various free-speech absolutists, civil liberties organizations, legal scholars, and libertarian thinkers. Below are the main arguments as presented by their proponents.

1. Free Speech Absolutism

The strongest version of this argument holds that the First Amendment (and equivalent protections elsewhere) should be interpreted without carve-outs for content based on its subject matter. Proponents argue:

  • Content-based restrictions are inherently suspect. The government should not have the power to declare certain ideas, images, or expressions inherently unworthy of protection.
  • Once a category of "unprotected speech" exists, it expands. Historically, obscenity exceptions have been used to prosecute materials addressing contraception, homosexuality, interracial relationships, and works by figures like James Joyce, Lady Chatterley's Lover, and Henry Miller.
  • The "marketplace of ideas" principle holds that citizens, not the state, should determine what speech has value.

2. The Subjectivity Problem

Justice Stewart's famous quip—"I know it when I see it"—is cited by critics as revealing the fundamental flaw:

  • Community standards vary wildly. What is obscene in one jurisdiction may be mainstream in another, creating arbitrary enforcement.
  • Standards shift over time. Works once banned (classical literature, anatomical drawings, Ulysses) are now taught in schools.
  • There's no objective definition. This means prosecutors, judges, and juries impose their personal or moral views on everyone.
  • This violates the rule of law principle that citizens should be able to know in advance what is prohibited.

3. The Chilling Effect on Art and Literature

This argument focuses on the collateral damage of obscenity laws:

  • Self-censorship by creators. Writers, filmmakers, and artists avoid exploring sexuality, the body, or transgressive themes to avoid prosecution.
  • Obscures important work. Literary and artistic movements that engage with sexuality—surrealism, body art, queer cinema, confessional writing—face disproportionate legal risk.
  • Harms marginalized voices especially. Gay and lesbian artists historically faced the brunt of obscenity prosecutions for materials that were simply depictions of their existence.
  • Educational and scientific materials get caught up. Anatomical texts, sex education, and HIV prevention materials have all been targeted.

4. The Harm Principle (Millian Liberalism)

Drawing from John Stuart Mill's On Liberty:

  • The only justification for restricting expression is preventing direct harm to others. Mere offense, moral disapproval, or "corrupting" effects on the viewer's character are not sufficient.
  • Adults should be presumed capable of consenting to view material. Paternalism—that the state must protect citizens from their own choices—undermines autonomy.
  • No conclusive evidence exists that adult consumption of explicit material directly causes the harms historically alleged.

5. Bodily Autonomy and Sexual Expression

This argument comes particularly from feminist and sex-positive traditions:

  • Sexual expression is a form of speech. Restricting it treats sexuality as inherently shameful.
  • Consensual adult sexual content involves no victim. The state has no proper interest in regulating it.
  • Criminalization creates real harms by driving the industry underground, away from labor protections, health standards, and accountability.
  • It disproportionately targets queer and feminist work that centers women's and LGBTQ+ pleasure.

6. Selective Enforcement and Class Bias

Critics argue obscenity laws are applied unequally:

  • The wealthy and well-connected rarely face prosecution. Small distributors, marginalized communities, and unpopular creators bear the brunt.
  • Prosecutors use obscenity charges selectively against political opponents, religious minorities, or disfavored groups.
  • The same content in a gallery may be legal but illegal in a bookstore—a distinction without meaningful principle.

7. The "Slippery Slope" of Definitions

The argument that obscenity exceptions expand:

  • Once a government can ban one type of speech based on content, what stops it from banning others? The "fighting words," "incitement," and "obscenity" exceptions have all been expanded.
  • Modern obscenity law already requires weighing "literary, artistic, political, or scientific value"—a judgment the state is ill-equipped to make.

8. Underground Market Harms

A practical libertarian argument:

  • Prohibition doesn't eliminate demand; it eliminates safety and accountability. Alcohol prohibition is the classic analogy.
  • Legal, regulated markets allow worker protections, health screening, age verification, and tax revenue.
  • Black markets correlate with exploitation because they cannot be policed by labor or health authorities.

9. Works That Were Wrongly Censored

Proponents point to a historical record as evidence:

  • Lady Chatterley's Lover, Lolita, Tropic of Cancer, works by the Marquis de Sade, Robert Mapplethorpe's photography, Mapplethorpe, Andres Serrano's Piss Christ (controversially), the works of Mapplethorpe, John Cleland's Fanny Hill, and the films of Pasolini and Bertolucci were all prosecuted or banned.
  • The "I know it when I see it" test has produced a long list of cultural embarrassments for the legal system.

A Note on Contested Ground

It's worth noting that this view is actively contested. Opponents argue that obscenity laws protect women from exploitation, shield children from exposure, preserve public decency, and reflect democratic moral consensus. Many feminists, religious groups, and anti-trafficking organizations hold opposing views. Defenders of obscenity law argue it's a narrow, judicially-controlled exception, not a tool of broad censorship.

The debate ultimately involves competing visions of how robust free expression should be, who should make decisions about sexual content, and how to weigh liberty against other social values.

A Speech on Free Speech and the Case Against Pornography Restrictions

Delivered to the assembled advocates of liberty

Friends, fellow citizens, lovers of liberty—

I stand before you today to defend a principle that is older than any nation, more fundamental than any statute, and more sacred than any comfort we derive from its absence. I speak of the right to think, to speak, to create, and to consume ideas and expression without the heavy hand of government deciding what we may see, read, or imagine.

For too long, we have allowed a peculiar and cowardly exception to fester at the heart of our free speech tradition. We proclaim, with great fanfare, our commitment to the First Amendment—and then we quietly carve out a category of expression we are willing to abandon to prosecutors, to moral panics, and to the shifting tastes of whoever holds power. That category is sexual expression. And the laws we have built around it are a betrayal of everything we claim to believe.

I. The Inconsistency is the Scandal

Tell me, friends—where did we get the idea that the human body, in its most intimate and vulnerable form, is somehow more dangerous to the republic than political lies, violent video games, grim literature, or religious tracts that promise damnation? Where did we acquire the confidence to declare that depictions of consensual adult activity are so uniquely corrupting that they must be hunted, prosecuted, and buried?

The answer is historical accident. The answer is Puritanism dressed up as law. The answer is a coalition of busybodies who have, generation after generation, convinced themselves that their private discomfort is a public virtue.

But liberty cannot survive on inconsistency. A right that applies only to speech we find agreeable is no right at all—it is a permission slip, revocable at the will of the majority. The true test of a free speech principle is not how it treats the popular, the polite, or the comfortable. It is how it treats the deviant, the explicit, and the disturbing.

II. The Harm Argument Has Failed

For decades, the defenders of censorship have asked us to weigh their claims of harm against the abstract value of liberty. And for decades, the evidence has refused to cooperate with them. The commissions have been convened. The studies have been funded. The moral entrepreneurs have testified. And what have they produced? A body of work that is contested, inconclusive, and perpetually in need of new funding.

Meanwhile, the actual practice of censorship has produced a long, disgraceful record: works of genuine artistic merit destroyed, careers ruined, libraries purged, and human beings branded as criminals for the crime of looking, drawing, writing, or filming.

When the censors cannot show clear, demonstrable harm, the burden shifts entirely to them. The default in a free society is permission, not prohibition. If you wish to ban speech, you must make the case—and the censors have not made it. They have only ever made appeals to disgust.

III. The Artist and the Citizen

Consider the artist. Consider the writer who wishes to describe the full range of human experience. Consider the filmmaker who refuses to flinch. Consider the illustrator, the photographer, the cartoonist, the student of history who must look honestly at the erotic art of past civilizations.

Under our current regime, every one of these creators walks a tightrope over a canyon. They are told: you may approach the human body, but not too closely. You may describe desire, but not too vividly. You may depict intimacy, but only in the sanitized language approved by a prosecutor's office in some distant county.

This is not a climate of free expression. This is a climate of self-censorship, where the chilling effect does the work that the law cannot openly do. The result is a culture that is poorer, more timid, and more dishonest about the realities of human life.

IV. The Tyranny of "Community Standards"

And here we must speak plainly about the most insidious provision in our obscenity laws: the "community standards" test. This is the clause that allows twelve people in some small town, or nine justices in some distant capital, to dictate what adults in a vast and diverse nation may view in the privacy of their own homes.

It is, in plain language, rule by the most prudish among us. It is the elevation of the most easily offended into censors for everyone. It tells the citizens of a great and pluralistic country that their rights are not their own—that they are leased from the sensibilities of strangers.

No free person should accept this. No free person can accept this without surrendering the very meaning of freedom.

V. What We Are Really Defending

Let us be clear about what we are defending when we defend unrestricted speech in this domain. We are defending the right of adults to make their own moral choices about what they read, view, and imagine. We are defending artists from the tyranny of those who would rather destroy a work than confront it. We are defending the principle that government has no business in the bedrooms, the bookshelves, or the imaginations of its citizens.

We are not arguing that everyone must consume this material. We are not arguing that anyone must approve of it. We are not arguing against the right of individuals, families, or communities to hold whatever views they wish about sexuality, morality, or art.

We are arguing that law—the blunt, coercive instrument of the state—has no legitimate role in enforcing those views upon everyone else.

VI. The Call to Action

So what do we ask? We ask for the repeal of every statute that makes a crime of consensual sexual expression among adults. We ask for the dismantling of every commission, every registry, every prosecutorial unit dedicated to chasing what consenting adults create and view in private. We ask for a return to first principles: that the freedom of speech means all speech, and that the freedom of the press means the freedom to print what the powerful wish would go unprinted.

We ask for courage—the courage to defend a principle even when it is unpopular, even when it is uncomfortable, even when it requires us to sit beside speech that offends us in order to preserve speech that does not.

VII. A Final Word

The great free speech traditions of the world were not built by men and women who only defended the speech they loved. They were built by those who understood that the alternative to a broad and sometimes troubling freedom is not a clean and safe society—it is a society where the censor's pen is the only pen that matters.

If we mean what we say when we invoke liberty, then we must mean it here. We must mean it when the subject is uncomfortable. We must mean it when the art is explicit. We must mean it when the speech is about the oldest, most universal, and most fiercely private of human experiences.

The freedom to imagine is not a concession. It is the foundation. And it is long past time we stopped pretending otherwise.

Thank you.
